questions.question: Which foods give you the most cadmium?
questions.answer: The foods that contribute most to overall cadmium exposure are everyday staples eaten in large volume rather than the most contaminated ones: cereals like rice and wheat, potatoes and starchy roots, leafy vegetables, nuts, oilseeds, pulses, and meat ([[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]], [[sources/jecfa-91st-cadmium-2022|JECFA 91st]]). Separately, the highest-concentration foods are bivalve molluscs other than oysters, wild mushrooms, cocoa and chocolate, seaweed, fungi, oilseeds, and organ meats such as kidney and liver ([[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Regular consumers of bivalve molluscs average 4.6 µg/kg body weight per week and regular wild-mushroom eaters 4.3, both well above the EFSA population mean of 2.3.

questions.question: Why is cadmium considered harmful and where does it build up in the body?
questions.answer: Cadmium is a non-essential heavy metal that is retained in the kidney and liver with a biological half-life of decades, so body burden accumulates across a lifetime and is never meaningfully excreted ([[sources/nordberg2015-cadmium-chapter|Nordberg 2015]]). Its main toxic effect is renal tubular dysfunction, with bone demineralization (osteomalacia, osteoporosis, and fracture risk) as a secondary endpoint ([[sources/nordberg2015-cadmium-chapter|Nordberg 2015]], [[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). It is also classified by IARC as a Group 1 human carcinogen based on occupational inhalation studies. There is no effective clinical treatment once cadmium accumulates, which is why exposure reduction is the appropriate response ([[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle and Barchowsky 2021]]).

questions.question: Who is most at risk from dietary cadmium?
questions.answer: Children aged 0.5 to 12 have mean dietary exposure about 60 percent higher than adults because they eat more food per unit body weight, and with cocoa products their total intake can reach 96 percent of the JECFA reference value ([[sources/jecfa-91st-cadmium-2022|JECFA 91st]]). Women of reproductive age with low iron stores absorb cadmium more efficiently, and pregnant women appear to accumulate more than nonpregnant women ([[sources/nordberg2015-cadmium-chapter|Nordberg 2015]], [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle and Barchowsky 2021]]). Postmenopausal women, vegetarians, regular consumers of bivalve molluscs or wild mushrooms, and smokers also carry elevated exposure; smoking roughly doubles body burden ([[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]], [[sources/nordberg2015-cadmium-chapter|Nordberg 2015]]).

questions.question: What are the official limits and safe-intake values for cadmium?
questions.answer: Four major bodies set dietary reference values: ATSDR's chronic oral Minimal Risk Level of 0.1 µg/kg/day (tightest), EFSA's tolerable weekly intake of 2.5 µg/kg body weight per week, JECFA's provisional tolerable monthly intake of 25 µg/kg body weight per month, and the US EPA IRIS oral reference dose of about 1.0 µg/kg/day for food ([[sources/atsdr-cadmium-toxprofile-2012|ATSDR 2012]], [[regulations/efsa-cadmium-twi|EFSA TWI]], [[regulations/jecfa-cadmium-ptmi|JECFA PTMI]]). Roughly a tenfold range separates them, reflecting different methodological choices on overlapping data rather than disagreement on the underlying toxicology. There are also binding maximum levels in food, such as EU limits and Codex matrix limits like 0.4 mg/kg for polished rice ([[sources/codex-cxs-193-1995|Codex CXS 193-1995]]).

questions.question: How is cadmium measured in food and in people?
questions.answer: Occurrence and biomonitoring studies use methods spanning flame atomic absorption spectrometry through ICP-MS, whose detection limits differ by four orders of magnitude, so pooled datasets must be handled carefully to avoid false precision ([[sources/atsdr-cadmium-toxprofile-2012|ATSDR 2012]]). FDA's Toxic Elements Program and ATSDR biomonitoring both use ICP-MS methods. For people, exposure is assessed by measuring cadmium in whole blood (recent exposure) or urine normalized to creatinine (cumulative body burden); the EFSA, ATSDR, and JECFA derivations all use urinary cadmium as the exposure metric ([[sources/jakubowski2012-zinc-cadmium-chapter|Jakubowski 2012]]).

questions.question: What can I actually do to lower my cadmium exposure?
questions.answer: Because the biggest population contributors are nutritional staples like rice, wheat, potatoes, and leafy vegetables, the guidance is not to avoid staples but to manage the high-concentration foods and behaviors that push you above average ([[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Moderating frequent cocoa and chocolate consumption is the single highest-leverage step for children under 12 ([[sources/jecfa-91st-cadmium-2022|JECFA 91st]]). Limiting regular bivalve molluscs, wild mushrooms, and organ meats, not smoking, and correcting iron deficiency (which raises cadmium absorption) all reduce exposure ([[sources/nordberg2015-cadmium-chapter|Nordberg 2015]], [[sources/ufelle2021-metals-chapter|Ufelle and Barchowsky 2021]]).
